title: Simulation-Based Empirical Bayes
abstract: Empirical Bayes (EB) performs simultaneous inference across many related latent variables. Classical EB assumes that the likelihood p(x | z) is tractable. In many scientific applications, however, the likelihood is available only through a simulator. This paper develops EB for such implicit likelihoods. We introduce simulation-based empirical Bayes (SBEB), which connects nonparametric EB to simulation-based inference (SBI). SBEB computes EB estimates without an explicit density by using the observed data, simulator samples, and an amortized inference network. SBEB iteratively refines the fitted EB prior toward the population prior. With several scientific simulators and real-world data, we demonstrate that SBEB improves accuracy over SBI with a fixed prior.

Blei Departments of Computer Science and Statistics Columbia University Abstract Empirical Bayes (EB) performs simultaneous inference across many related latent variables. Classical EB assumes that the likelihood p ​ ( x | z ) \mathrm{p}(x\,|\,z) is tractable. In many scientific applications, however, the likelihood is available only through a simulator. This paper develops EB for such implicit likelihoods. We introduce simulation-based empirical Bayes (SBEB), which connects nonparametric EB to simulation-based inference (SBI). SBEB computes EB estimates without an explicit density by using the observed data, simulator samples, and an amortized inference network. SBEB iteratively refines the fitted EB prior toward the population prior. With several scientific simulators and real-world data, we demonstrate that SBEB improves accuracy over SBI with a fixed prior. 1 Introduction Figure 1 : Biweekly measles reports from six UK cities. Each panel is one city. The full dataset contains 40 cities observed from 1944 to 1965 (Dalziel et al. , 2016 ) . This paper is about simultaneous inference with simulation-based likelihoods and empirical Bayes. As an example, Figure ˜ 1 shows biweekly measles reports from six UK cities, drawn from a dataset of 40 cities. The trajectories show recurrent outbreaks, changes in amplitude, and city-to-city variation. To explain data like these, epidemiologists build mechanistic simulators (Finkenstädt and Grenfell, 2000 ; Bjørnstad et al. , 2002 ) . In such a simulator, the input is a vector of epidemic parameters for transmission, seasonality, and reporting. The output is a time series of reported cases. These epidemic simulators encode theories about how infections spread and are reported. Given data like those in Figure ˜ 1 , the statistical goal is to infer the epidemic parameters for each city. Formally, let x i x_{i} denote the observed time series for city i i , and let z i z_{i} denote its epidemic parameters. A Bayesian analysis targets p ​ ( z i | x i ) ∝ p ​ ( z i ) ​ p ​ ( x i | z i ) , \displaystyle\mathrm{p}(z_{i}\,|\,x_{i})\propto\mathrm{p}(z_{i})\mathrm{p}(x_{i}\,|\,z_{i}), where p ​ ( z ) \mathrm{p}(z) is a prior over simulation parameters and p ​ ( x | z ) \mathrm{p}(x\,|\,z) is the conditional likelihood of a trajectory induced by the simulator. This problem has two notable features. First, the likelihood is defined by simulation. For a proposed parameter z i z_{i} , the simulator can generate a time series x i x_{i} , but it cannot necessarily evaluate p ​ ( x i | z i ) \mathrm{p}(x_{i}\,|\,z_{i}) . Second, the problem is simultaneous. We have many related cities and many related inference problems. Their epidemic parameters differ, but they come from a common population. These two features of the problem suggest two statistical ideas. The first idea is simulation-based inference (SBI) (Cranmer et al. , 2020 ; Deistler et al. , 2025 ) . SBI uses simulator draws to approximate posterior inference when the likelihood cannot be evaluated. It has become a standard tool for scientific models where simulation is available but likelihood calculation is not. The SBI workflow begins by choosing a prior, drawing z b ∼ p ​ ( z ) z_{b}\sim\mathrm{p}(z) , simulating x b ∼ p ​ ( x | z b ) x_{b}\sim\mathrm{p}(x\,|\,z_{b}) , and fitting an amortized approximation q ​ ( z ; x ) \mathrm{q}(z\,;\,x) on these simulated pairs. In SBI, the prior plays its usual role in the posterior, but it is also used to draw the parameters used for simulation. The second idea is empirical Bayes (EB) (Robbins, 1956 ; Stein, 1956 ; Efron and Morris, 1973 ; Efron, 2014 , 2019 ) . EB uses the collection of observations to learn the prior for the latent parameters. This helps simultaneous inference in two ways. From a Bayesian view, the learned prior captures the population that generated the units. From a frequentist view, the learned prior shrinks noisy unit-level estimates toward the population and can improve repeated-sampling risk. In this paper, we combine these two ideas to develop simulation-based empirical Bayes (SBEB), a method that uses SBI to perform simultaneous inference with an EB prior. SBEB refines an approximate nonparametric EB prior and samples from it inside an SBI loop. The result is EB analysis for intractable, simulation-based likelihoods. SBEB extends both SBI and EB. In standard SBI, the prior is fixed before simulation and training (Cranmer et al. , 2020 ; Deistler et al. , 2025 ) . SBEB instead learns a flexible prior from the data, while it performs simulation-based inference. Classical EB methods usually rely on simple, explicit likelihoods, such as Gaussian normal-means models (Stein, 1956 ; Efron and Morris, 1973 ) or Poisson models (Robbins, 1956 ; Bühlmann, 1967 ) . SBEB extends empirical Bayes to implicit likelihoods based on complex simulators. After developing SBEB, we study it theoretically and empirically. Theoretically, we study an oracle version and prove that it converges to the population prior, i.e., the prior whose induced marginal distribution of observations matches the population. Empirically, we first study SBEB in controlled simulators, where the true latent variables are known. We then study two real datasets: discrete choice models for product choices by people (Allenby et al. , 2014a , b ) and epidemic simulators for measles time series by cities (Dalziel et al. , 2016 ) . Across these studies, SBEB improves on classical SBI with a fixed prior. 2 Simulation-based empirical Bayes We develop the method in three steps. First, we review empirical Bayes (EB) for simultaneous inference and define the population prior. Second, we review simulation-based inference (SBI), which fits an amortized posterior approximation from simulator draws. Finally, we develop simulation-based empirical Bayes (SBEB). It iteratively uses simulation-based inference to approximate posterior distributions, and then uses those posteriors to refine an empirical Bayes prior. 2.1 Empirical Bayes and the population prior Consider a model with local latent variables, p ​ ( z , x ) = p ​ ( z ) ​ p ​ ( x | z ) . \displaystyle\mathrm{p}(z,x)=\mathrm{p}(z)\mathrm{p}(x\,|\,z). (1) We observe a dataset 𝐱 = x 1 : n \mathbf{x}=x_{1:n} . Our goal is simultaneous inference of 𝐳 = z 1 : n \mathbf{z}=z_{1:n} , p ​ ( 𝐳 | 𝐱 ) = ∏ i = 1 n p ​ ( z i | x i ) . \displaystyle\mathrm{p}(\mathbf{z}\,|\,\mathbf{x})=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{p}(z_{i}\,|\,x_{i}). (2) This problem involves n n posterior inferences. The prior p ​ ( z ) \mathrm{p}(z) ties these inferences together. The empirical Bayes question is: what should the prior p ​ ( z ) \mathrm{p}(z) be? Suppose our data came from a true population distribution, x i ​ ∼ i . i . d . ​ p ⋆ ​ ( x ) x_{i}\overset{\rm i.i.d.}{\sim}\mathrm{p}^{\star}(x) . The empirical Bayes criterion says that the model marginal should match the true population distribution, p ⋆ ​ ( x ) = p ​ ( x ) , \displaystyle\mathrm{p}^{\star}(x)=\mathrm{p}(x), (3) where the marginal is p ​ ( x ) = ∫ p ​ ( z ) ​ p ​ ( x | z ) ​ d z . \displaystyle\mathrm{p}(x)=\int\mathrm{p}(z)\,\mathrm{p}(x\,|\,z)\,\mathrm{d}z. (4) The goal of empirical Bayes is to set the prior p ​ ( z ) \mathrm{p}(z) so that the EB criterion holds (Robbins, 1956 ; Efron, 2019 ) . A prior that satisfies the EB criterion can be written as an expectation over the posterior, p ​ ( z ) = 𝔼 p ⋆ ​ ( x ) ​ [ p ​ ( z | x ) ] . \displaystyle\mathrm{p}(z)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{p}^{\star}(x)}\left[\mathrm{p}(z\,|\,x)\right]. (5) We call this prior the population prior . The equation is an identity: the prior p ​ ( z ) \mathrm{p}(z) appears on both sides because the posterior p ​ ( z | x ) \mathrm{p}(z\,|\,x) is computed under that same prior. Related posterior-averaging forms appear in nonparametric empirical Bayes and amortized variational inference (Laird, 1978 ; McInerney et al. , 2015 ; Tomczak and Welling, 2017 ) . We prove Eq. ˜ 5 in Appendix ˜ A . The identity in Eq. ˜ 5 does not define the prior directly; it gives a fixed point. But it suggests an algorithm: if we can approximate the posteriors p ​ ( z | x i ) \mathrm{p}(z\,|\,x_{i}) for the observed units, then we can approximate the population prior by averaging those posteriors. We use this idea to develop SBEB in Section ˜ 2.3 . 2.2 Fixed-prior simulation-based inference Suppose we can simulate from p ​ ( x | z ) \mathrm{p}(x\,|\,z) but cannot evaluate its density. For now, suppose the prior p ​ ( z ) \mathrm{p}(z) is fixed. (We will return to EB later.) This subsection explains fixed-prior simulation-based inference in three steps: the amortized family, the training objective, and the simulator-based Monte Carlo approximation. Given a dataset 𝐱 \mathbf{x} , how can we perform simultaneous inference? One strategy is simulation-based inference (SBI) (Papamakarios et al. , 2019 ; Cranmer et al. , 2020 ) . A common SBI approach, neural posterior estimation, uses simulated data to fit an inference network q ​ ( z ; x , φ ) \mathrm{q}(z\,;\,x,\varphi) that approximates the posterior for any observation x x . For the observed units, we use q ​ ( z ; x i , φ ) \mathrm{q}(z\,;\,x_{i},\varphi) as an approximation to p ​ ( z | x i ) \mathrm{p}(z\,|\,x_{i}) . The inference network is amortized: the same parameter vector φ \varphi is used for all observations. The network takes an observation x x as input and returns a distribution over z z . For example, the output might be the mean and covariance of a Gaussian distribution, or the parameters of a more flexible conditional density model. Neural networks and normalizing flows are common choices (Papamakarios and Murray, 2016 ; Greenberg et al. , 2019 ) . The target is the exact posterior p ​ ( z | x ) \mathrm{p}(z\,|\,x) , averaged over the kinds of observations generated by the model. We fit the inference parameters φ \varphi by optimizing the SBI objective, ℒ ​ ( φ ) = 𝔼 p ​ ( x ) ​ [ KL ​ ( p ​ ( z | x ) ∥ q ​ ( z ; x , φ ) ) ] . \displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\varphi)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{p}(x)}\left[\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathrm{p}(z\,|\,x)\,\|\,\mathrm{q}(z\,;\,x,\varphi)\right)\right]. (6) It is the expected KL divergence between the exact and approximate posteriors, where the expectation is with respect to the marginal distribution of the observation. The key idea behind SBI is that the same joint distribution can be written in two ways, p ​ ( x ) ​ p ​ ( z | x ) = p ​ ( z ) ​ p ​ ( x | z ) \mathrm{p}(x)\mathrm{p}(z\,|\,x)=\mathrm{p}(z)\mathrm{p}(x\,|\,z) . We cannot sample from p ​ ( x ) ​ p ​ ( z | x ) \mathrm{p}(x)\mathrm{p}(z\,|\,x) directly, because that would require posterior samples. But with a fixed prior and a simulator, we can sample from p ​ ( z ) ​ p ​ ( x | z ) \mathrm{p}(z)\mathrm{p}(x\,|\,z) . This lets us rewrite the objective, ℒ ​ ( φ ) \displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\varphi) = 𝔼 p ​ ( x ) ​ [ 𝔼 p ​ ( z | x ) ​ [ log ⁡ p ​ ( z | x ) − log ⁡ q ​ ( z ; x , φ ) ] ] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{p}(x)}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{p}(z\,|\,x)}\left[\log\mathrm{p}(z\,|\,x)-\log\mathrm{q}(z\,;\,x,\varphi)\right]\right] (7) = 𝔼 p ​ ( z , x ) ​ [ log ⁡ p ​ ( z | x ) − log ⁡ q ​ ( z ; x , φ ) ] . \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{p}(z,x)}\left[\log\mathrm{p}(z\,|\,x)-\log\mathrm{q}(z\,;\,x,\varphi)\right]. (8) Eq. ˜ 7 uses the definition of the KL divergence; Eq. ˜ 8 uses that p ​ ( z , x ) = p ​ ( x ) ​ p ​ ( z | x ) \mathrm{p}(z,x)=\mathrm{p}(x)\,\mathrm{p}(z\,|\,x) . We have now written the objective in terms of an expectation with respect to the joint. The first term in Eq. ˜ 8 does not depend on φ \varphi . We minimize the second term with a Monte Carlo approximation, arg ⁡ min φ ⁡ ℒ ​ ( φ ) \displaystyle\arg\min_{\varphi}\mathcal{L}(\varphi) = arg ⁡ min φ ⁡ 𝔼 p ​ ( z , x ) ​ [ − log ⁡ q ​ ( z ; x , φ ) ] \displaystyle=\arg\min_{\varphi}\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{p}(z,x)}\left[-\log\mathrm{q}(z\,;\,x,\varphi)\right] ≈ arg ⁡ min φ ⁡ 1 B ​ ∑ b − log ⁡ q ​ ( z b ; x b , φ ) z b , x b ∼ p ​ ( z ) ​ p ​ ( x | z ) . \displaystyle\approx\arg\min_{\varphi}\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b}-\log\mathrm{q}(z_{b}\,;\,x_{b},\varphi)\quad\quad z_{b},x_{b}\sim\mathrm{p}(z)\,\mathrm{p}(x\,|\,z). Thus fixed-prior SBI reduces posterior approximation to supervised learning on simulated pairs ( z b , x b ) (z_{b},x_{b}) . Algorithm ˜ 1 summarizes fixed-prior SBI. Its output is a fitted inference network φ ^ \hat{\varphi} . For each observed unit x i x_{i} , we approximate the posterior with q ​ ( z ; x i , φ ^ ) \mathrm{q}(z\,;\,x_{i},\hat{\varphi}) . The prior should be the population prior in Eq. ˜ 5 , but the likelihood is only available through simulation. We cannot use classical EB methods, which require evaluating p ​ ( x | z ) \mathrm{p}(x\,|\,z) , and we cannot use traditional SBI, which requires a pre-specified prior. Simulation-based empirical Bayes (SBEB) combines the two ideas: it learns an approximate population prior and uses it inside an SBI loop. SBEB works in rounds. At round t t , the current inference network gives an approximate posterior for each observed unit, q ​ ( z ; x i , φ ^ t − 1 ) \mathrm{q}(z\,;\,x_{i},\hat{\varphi}_{t-1}) . We average these approximate posteriors over the observed units: p ^ t ​ ( z ) = 𝔼 p ^ n ​ ( x ) ​ [ q ​ ( z ; x , φ ^ t − 1 ) ] = 1 n ​ ∑ i = 1 n q ​ ( z ; x i , φ ^ t − 1 ) . \displaystyle\hat{\mathrm{p}}_{t}(z)=\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\mathrm{p}}_{n}(x)}\left[\mathrm{q}(z\,;\,x,\hat{\varphi}_{t-1})\right]=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{q}(z\,;\,x_{i},\hat{\varphi}_{t-1}). (9) This is the sample analogue of the population-prior identity in Eq. ˜ 5 , where p ^ n ​ ( x ) \hat{\mathrm{p}}_{n}(x) denotes the empirical distribution of the observed data. The key point is that we can sample from p ^ t ​ ( z ) \hat{\mathrm{p}}_{t}(z) even though we do not have a closed-form formula for its density. To draw from it, sample an observed unit x i x_{i} uniformly from the dataset, and then draw z ∼ q ​ ( z ; x i , φ ^ t − 1 ) z\sim\mathrm{q}(z\,;\,x_{i},\hat{\varphi}_{t-1}) . Given this draw of z z , we simulate a new observation x ∼ p ​ ( x | z ) x\sim\mathrm{p}(x\,|\,z) . These simulated pairs train the next inference network. Algorithm ˜ 2 summarizes SBEB. It starts from an initial prior p 0 ​ ( z ) \mathrm{p}_{0}(z) and fits a fixed-prior SBI approximation. It then iteratively draws parameters from the approximate EB prior, simulates new observations, and refits the inference network. It returns posterior approximations under the learned population prior, { q ​ ( z ; x i , φ ^ T ) } i = 1 n \{\mathrm{q}(z\,;\,x_{i},\hat{\varphi}_{T})\}_{i=1}^{n} . We assume that the fitted inference network can represent the exact posterior under the current prior, and that population expectations are available. This separates the statistical idea from the numerical approximations in the algorithm. Under these assumptions, SBEB iterates a map on priors and moves toward the population prior. The proofs are provided in Appendix ˜ A . Let p t ​ ( z ) \mathrm{p}_{t}(z) be the prior at iteration t t , and let p t ​ ( x ) = ∫ p t ​ ( z ) ​ p ​ ( x | z ) ​ d z \mathrm{p}_{t}(x)=\int\mathrm{p}_{t}(z)\mathrm{p}(x\,|\,z)\,\mathrm{d}z be its induced model marginal. The posterior under this prior is p t ​ ( z | x ) = p t ​ ( z ) ​ p ​ ( x | z ) p t ​ ( x ) . \displaystyle\mathrm{p}_{t}(z\,|\,x)=\frac{\mathrm{p}_{t}(z)\mathrm{p}(x\,|\,z)}{\mathrm{p}_{t}(x)}. The population-prior identity in Eq. ˜ 5 suggests the update p t + 1 ​ ( z ) = 𝔼 p ⋆ ​ ( x ) ​ [ p t ​ ( z | x ) ] . \displaystyle\mathrm{p}_{t+1}(z)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{p}^{\star}(x)}\left[\mathrm{p}_{t}(z\,|\,x)\right]. (10) This is the population version of the SBEB update in Eq. ˜ 9 . The algorithm replaces the posterior p t ​ ( z | x ) \mathrm{p}_{t}(z\,|\,x) with an amortized approximation and replaces the population expectation with an average over observed units. The update in Eq. ˜ 10 is also an expectation-maximization (EM) update. To see this, we define the objective ℓ ​ ( p ​ ( z ) , q ​ ( z ; x , φ ) ) = 𝔼 p ⋆ ​ ( x ) ​ [ 𝔼 q ​ ( z ; x , φ ) ​ [ log ⁡ p ​ ( z ) ​ p ​ ( x | z ) q ​ ( z ; x , φ ) ] ] . \displaystyle\ell(\mathrm{p}(z),\mathrm{q}(z\,;\,x,\varphi))=\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{p}^{\star}(x)}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{q}(z\,;\,x,\varphi)}\left[\log\frac{\mathrm{p}(z)\mathrm{p}(x\,|\,z)}{\mathrm{q}(z\,;\,x,\varphi)}\right]\right]. (11) For a fixed prior p t ​ ( z ) \mathrm{p}_{t}(z) , maximizing ℓ \ell over q \mathrm{q} gives the posterior p t ​ ( z | x ) \mathrm{p}_{t}(z\,|\,x) . For a fixed posterior approximation, maximizing ℓ \ell over the prior gives the average posterior in Eq. ˜ 10 . The idealized SBEB update is coordinate ascent on this objective. We analyze the idealized SBEB update in three stages. First, we show that at every iteration, the update improves the fit of the induced marginal. Next, we show that the prior KL divergence decreases by at least the current marginal KL divergence; this result then implies convergence of the sequence of marginals to the population marginal. Finally, we introduce a prior identifiability condition under which marginal convergence leads to convergence of the sequence of priors. The first result says that the oracle update improves the model marginal distribution of the data. Proposition 1 (Monotonicity) . For the oracle update in Eq. ˜ 10 , it holds that 𝔼 p ⋆ ​ ( x ) ​ [ log ⁡ p t ​ ( x ) ] ≤ 𝔼 p ⋆ ​ ( x ) ​ [ log ⁡ p t + 1 ​ ( x ) ] , \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{p}^{\star}(x)}\left[\log\mathrm{p}_{t}(x)\right]\,\leq\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{p}^{\star}(x)}\left[\log\mathrm{p}_{t+1}(x)\right], Equivalently, the KL divergence from the population distribution to the model marginal decreases, KL ​ ( p ⋆ ​ ( x ) ∥ p t + 1 ​ ( x ) ) ≤ KL ​ ( p ⋆ ​ ( x ) ∥ p t ​ ( x ) ) . \displaystyle\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathrm{p}^{\star}(x)\,\|\,\mathrm{p}_{t+1}(x)\right)\,\leq\,\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathrm{p}^{\star}(x)\,\|\,\mathrm{p}_{t}(x)\right). (12) Now let p ⋆ ​ ( z ) \mathrm{p}^{\star}(z) be a population prior as defined in Eq. ˜ 5 , and let p ⋆ ​ ( x ) \mathrm{p}^{\star}(x) be its induced marginal. The next result says that each step also moves the prior toward the population prior. Proposition 2 (Prior descent) . For any t ≥ 0 t\geq 0 , KL ​ ( p ⋆ ​ ( z ) ∥ p t ​ ( z ) ) − KL ​ ( p ⋆ ​ ( z ) ∥ p t + 1 ​ ( z ) ) ≥ KL ​ ( p ⋆ ​ ( x ) ∥ p t ​ ( x ) ) . \displaystyle\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathrm{p}^{\star}(z)\,\|\,\mathrm{p}_{t}(z)\right)-\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathrm{p}^{\star}(z)\,\|\,\mathrm{p}_{t+1}(z)\right)\geq\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathrm{p}^{\star}(x)\,\|\,\mathrm{p}_{t}(x)\right). Together, the two propositions imply convergence of the model marginal. Let p 0 ​ ( z ) \mathrm{p}_{0}(z) be the initial prior. Corollary 1 (Marginal convergence) . Suppose that KL ​ ( p ⋆ ​ ( z ) ∥ p 0 ​ ( z ) ) < ∞ \mathrm{KL}\left(\mathrm{p}^{\star}(z)\,\|\,\mathrm{p}_{0}(z)\right)<\infty . Then KL ​ ( p ⋆ ​ ( x ) ∥ p t ​ ( x ) ) → 0 , as ​ t → ∞ . \displaystyle\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathrm{p}^{\star}(x)\,\|\,\mathrm{p}_{t}(x)\right)\to 0,\quad\textrm{as }\;t\to\infty. The convergence theorem for the prior needs one property of the simulator. If two priors are far apart, then their induced marginal distributions of the data must also be far apart. Otherwise the data cannot distinguish the priors. Definition 1 (Prior identifiability) . Let p a ​ ( z ) \mathrm{p}_{a}(z) and p b ​ ( z ) \mathrm{p}_{b}(z) be any two prior distributions. The corresponding marginal likelihoods after simulation are p a ​ ( x ) = ∫ p a ​ ( z ) ​ p ​ ( x | z ) ​ d z \mathrm{p}_{a}(x)=\int\mathrm{p}_{a}(z)\mathrm{p}(x\,|\,z)\,\mathrm{d}z and p b ​ ( x ) = ∫ p b ​ ( z ) ​ p ​ ( x | z ) ​ d z \mathrm{p}_{b}(x)=\int\mathrm{p}_{b}(z)\mathrm{p}(x\,|\,z)\,\mathrm{d}z . We say that the simulator is prior-identifiable if p a ​ ( x ) = p b ​ ( x ) , ∀ x ⇒ p a ​ ( z ) = p b ​ ( z ) , ∀ z . \mathrm{p}_{a}(x)=\mathrm{p}_{b}(x),\;\forall\,x\quad\Rightarrow\quad\mathrm{p}_{a}(z)=\mathrm{p}_{b}(z),\;\forall\,z. We say it is λ \lambda -strongly prior-identifiable, under KL divergence, if KL ​ ( p a ​ ( z ) ∥ p b ​ ( z ) ) ≤ 1 λ ​ KL ​ ( p a ​ ( x ) ∥ p b ​ ( x ) ) . \mathrm{KL}\left(\mathrm{p}_{a}(z)\,\|\,\mathrm{p}_{b}(z)\right)\,\leq\,\tfrac{1}{\lambda}\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathrm{p}_{a}(x)\,\|\,\mathrm{p}_{b}(x)\right). Remark . The simulator maps priors on z z to marginals on x x through the Markov kernel p ​ ( x | z ) \mathrm{p}(x\,|\,z) . By the data processing inequality for KL divergence (Cover and Thomas, 2006 ) , KL ​ ( p a ​ ( x ) ∥ p b ​ ( x ) ) ≤ KL ​ ( p a ​ ( z ) ∥ p b ​ ( z ) ) . \displaystyle\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathrm{p}_{a}(x)\,\|\,\mathrm{p}_{b}(x)\right)\leq\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathrm{p}_{a}(z)\,\|\,\mathrm{p}_{b}(z)\right). Thus λ \lambda -strong prior-identifiability is an inverse data-processing condition, so it can hold only with λ ≤ 1 \lambda\leq 1 . This condition may hold only locally, when the two priors are close: for some R > 0 R>0 , KL ​ ( p a ​ ( z ) ∥ p b ​ ( z ) ) ≤ R \mathrm{KL}\left(\mathrm{p}_{a}(z)\,\|\,\mathrm{p}_{b}(z)\right)\leq R . The convergence result below still holds in this local form when the initial prior is close to the population prior. Ordinary prior-identifiability gives a qualitative consequence of Corollary ˜ 1 . By Pinsker’s inequality, the marginal KL convergence implies convergence in total variation, and hence weak convergence, of p t ​ ( x ) \mathrm{p}_{t}(x) to p ⋆ ​ ( x ) \mathrm{p}^{\star}(x) . If the priors are tight and the simulator maps weakly convergent priors to weakly convergent marginals, then every weak limit point of p t ​ ( z ) \mathrm{p}_{t}(z) must induce p ⋆ ​ ( x ) \mathrm{p}^{\star}(x) ; by prior-identifiability, that limit point is p ⋆ ​ ( z ) \mathrm{p}^{\star}(z) . Thus the priors converge weakly, though not under a specified metric or at a specified rate. Stronger identifiability gives more: it quantifies how marginal discrepancy controls prior discrepancy. The next theorem uses this condition to obtain geometric convergence of the prior under the oracle update. Theorem 1 . When the simulator identifies the prior and the posterior approximation is exact, the population-prior update moves geometrically toward the population prior. The SBEB algorithm approximates this update with a finite dataset and amortized posterior family. 4 Related work Empirical Bayes. Empirical Bayes (EB) estimates prior structure from data by matching model and population behavior. Classical EB ideas go back to Robbins ( 1956 ) ; for a modern perspective, see Efron ( 2019 ) . The empirical Bayes criterion ( Eq. ˜ 3 ) follows this line: set the prior so that the model marginal equals the population distribution. Amortized variational inference and the population prior. Amortized inference fits a shared inference function across observations or datasets. Several papers work with the population prior, sometimes under different names. The population posterior of McInerney et al. ( 2015 ) averages posterior distributions across data streams. The amortized population posterior of Goyal et al. ( 2017 ) learns inference across a population of datasets. The VampPrior of Tomczak and Welling ( 2017 ) represents a prior as a mixture of variational posteriors evaluated at learned pseudo-observations. These methods show that posterior averages can define useful priors. Simulation-based inference. Simulation-based inference (SBI) uses simulators for models whose likelihoods cannot be evaluated. Early approaches include approximate Bayesian computation (Beaumont et al. , 2002 ; Sisson et al. , 2018 ) . Neural SBI methods train conditional density models from simulated pairs, including neural posterior estimation (Papamakarios and Murray, 2016 ; Greenberg et al. , 2019 ) , neural likelihood estimation (Papamakarios et al. , 2019 ) , and related methods (Wildberger et al. , 2023 ; Hikida et al. , 2025 ) . Broader surveys and benchmarks appear in Cranmer et al. ( 2020 ); Lueckmann et al. ( 2021 ); Tejero–Cantero et al. ( 2020 ) . Sequential SBI adapts the simulation distribution over rounds (Papamakarios and Murray, 2016 ; Lueckmann et al. , 2017 ; Greenberg et al. , 2019 ) . It focuses simulation on the observed data, so that the fitted posterior approximation is accurate where it will be used. SBEB also changes the simulation distribution over rounds and also focuses simulation on the observed units. But it does so while fitting an empirical Bayes prior. This gives a simpler algorithm in one sense: SBEB samples from the current prior estimate and does not need to reweight samples to correct back to a fixed prior. Likelihood-free source distribution estimation. Some SBI papers call the unknown prior the source distribution . In this language, source distribution estimation is close to empirical Bayes. Neural empirical Bayes (Vandegar et al. , 2021 ) first learns a neural surrogate likelihood from simulated pairs. It then fits a parameterized generative model for the source distribution by optimizing an estimate of the marginal likelihood. Sourcerer (Vetter et al. , 2024 ) takes a different route: it is sample-based, targets a maximum-entropy source distribution, and uses sliced-Wasserstein distance to compare observed data to simulations. SBEB differs from both approaches. It does not first learn a surrogate likelihood, and it does not solve a separate source-estimation problem. Instead, it keeps prior learning and posterior approximation in one loop. Each round samples from the current average posterior, simulates new data, and refits the amortized posterior approximation. The fixed point is the population-prior identity in Eq. ˜ 5 . 5 Empirical studies We evaluate simulation-based empirical Bayes (SBEB) in three settings. The first setting is a suite of controlled simulation studies, where the latent variables are known and we can directly measure how well we recover them. The second and third settings are real-data studies: heterogeneous product choice and childhood measles dynamics. In the real-data studies, the latent variables are not observed, so we evaluate by holding out data from each unit and asking how well the inferred unit-specific parameters predict the held-out observations. Across studies, a unit i i has observed data x i x_{i} and a latent parameter z i z_{i} . Fixed-prior SBI trains the amortized posterior from a fixed prior ( Algorithm ˜ 1 ). SBEB starts from the same prior and then uses the collection of observed units to estimate an empirical Bayes prior while training the amortized posterior ( Algorithm ˜ 2 ). The real-data comparisons also include a per-unit method that does not share information across units. 5.1 Simulation studies We first study SBEB in simulation, where we know the latent variables that produced the data. Discrete choice models are a standard tool in econometrics (McFadden, 1974 ; Train, 2009 ) .
